awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of a Cloud Laboratory Platform for Laboratory Automation
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project focuses on the development of automated laboratories for the remote execution of scientific experiments. Automated laboratories allow scientists to submit and manage their experiments over the internet, eliminating the need for a physical presence in a traditional laboratory setting. Currently, traditional laboratories involve significant upfront investments in equipment, resources, and dedicated laboratory spaces, making research costly and limiting accessibility, especially for smaller research teams and educational institutions. By removing these barriers, automated laboratories significantly reduce the cost and complexity of conducting scientific research, enabling participation from researchers in academia, startups, and industry. The widespread adoption of automated laboratories would enhance the reproducibility of scientific research, accelerate innovation across the life sciences, and support national interests by facilitating advancements in healthcare, biotechnology, and pharmaceuticals.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. This solution is based on the development of a cloud-based laboratory platform integrating robotics, automation software, and artificial intelligence-driven systems. The core of this technology involves a programming language specifically designed to describe detailed experimental protocols, which the platform translates into precise instructions executed by robotic instruments and laboratory personnel. Users benefit from unprecedented accuracy, reproducibility, and data transparency, greatly facilitating analysis and collaboration. Furthermore, the integration of advanced artificial intelligence models aids researchers in experimental design, result interpretation, and logistical management. Adoption of this technology will enable researchers to scale their experiments rapidly, conduct parallel experiments efficiently, and significantly streamline the path from hypothesis to discovery.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This NSF I-Corps project at Columbia University explored the commercial potential of a cloud laboratory: a facility where researchers could request experiments remotely and have them carried out using laboratory automation. The project examined how this approach could meet needs in life-science research. Through customer-discovery interviews—conversations with potential users and purchasing decision makers—the team focused its investigation on automated chemical synthesis for drug discovery. In this application, the proposed service would supply custom small molecules that scientists use to test and develop potential medicines. The team spoke with people at biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies across the United States, including both small firms and large organizations, to understand their needs and evaluate assumptions about a future service.

The interviews identified delivery turnaround time as a major concern among prospective customers. Delays in obtaining molecules can hold up the next round of experiments. The team learned that the value of faster delivery depended on customers’ testing schedules: some organizations planned their experiments around shipments arriving at the start of the week. As a result, saving a few days would not necessarily accelerate testing; delivery improvements needed to enable an earlier weekly testing cycle. These findings informed a proposed service target of delivering molecules one to two weeks faster. Interviews also challenged the team’s initial assumption that concerns about intellectual-property security would be a primary reason to change suppliers. Among the decision makers interviewed, this concern was less prominent than expected. Some larger organizations instead emphasized diversifying the geographic locations of their suppliers. These findings helped the team refine its intended customer groups and prioritize the benefits a future service would need to demonstrate.

The project’s principal outcome was a more specific, evidence-based understanding of a potential application for laboratory automation and the requirements for its adoption. It also gave graduate-student team members practical experience in interviewing potential customers, testing business assumptions, and translating scientific capabilities into a proposed commercial service. The findings provide a basis for future technology development and evaluation. If realized, a service that reliably shortens molecule-delivery times could help research teams complete drug-discovery experiments sooner. This potential benefit remains a goal for subsequent development and validation.
